utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Thank you, Your Honour. Our next witness is Sasa Antic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Antic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, and make yourself as comfortable as you can; we appreciate that special arrangements are necessary to ensure that. It doesn't look very comfortable from here, but ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot make myself more comfortable than this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... on behalf of Mr. Lazarevic. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Antic, good morning.

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Would you please state your full name for the record, your date and place of birth for the record.

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: My name is Sasa Antic. I was born 3rd July 1970 in Gnjilane.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Antic, did you give a statement to this Defence team on the 5th of January, 2008?

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to review this statement, to read it, and sign it?

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Does it reflect everything that you stated to the Defence team of General Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: If we were to ask you the same questions today, would you provide the same answers?

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Antic, this Court and the Office of the Prosecutor and my colleagues from other Defence teams are in possession of your statement; therefore, it would not be necessary to repeat what is contained in it. I would only like to ask you some additional questions, or rather, to clarify certain points.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before that I would kindly request that this statement, which is Defence Exhibit 5D1398 be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Antic, you said you were born in Gnjilane. Gnjilane is in the province of Kosovo and Metohija, correct?

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the eastern part of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In paragraph 14 you stated that together with some civilians of Albanian ethnicity you discussed the reasons why they were leaving their places of residence, and some of them told you that they would go either to Macedonia or to Gnjilane. Did you have occasion during the war before and during the NATO air-strikes to go to Gnjilane; and if so, how often?

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. My entire family lives in the broader area of Gnjilane, more precisely in a village which is around 15 kilometres away from Gnjilane itself. Before the war, as often as I was able to, I went to visit my family; and during the war, I believe I was able to visit three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In Gnjilane and around it, were there any civilians before and during the NATO air-strikes and were there more during the air-strikes?

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: You could observe in the streets that there were many more civilians than resided there before the war began.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Antic. In paragraphs 15 and 16 of your statement, you said something about the losses of the battalion where you served. Could you tell me, if you know, how many men were killed from your battalion during the war and how many were wounded?

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: In my battalion, specifically in my company, because they were all members of my company, a total of 15 men were killed, 13 soldiers, one NCO, and one officer. And there was certainly more than 20 members of the battalion who were wounded. I cannot give you the exact number, but it's certainly over 20, between 20 and 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 16, you described an incident on the road from Klina to Djakovica where part of the unit of the 52nd Military Police Battalion was bombed. You said five soldiers were killed as well as NCO Boban Milic. Do you know if an officer from the command of the Pristina Corps was killed on that occasion as well?

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes. On that occasion in a combat vehicle of the infantry there was Lieutenant-Colonel Simovic from the command of the Pristina Corps, but I cannot tell exactly which position he occupied in the command. He was killed together with those five soldiers and with my second lieutenant, Milic, who was also deputy commander of my company.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Antic. In paragraph 22, you described an assignment on the 27th and 28th of April in a valley called Caragoj or Reka valley. You said that you had received an assignment to move your forces on the 27th and 28th of April, including a part of your company, in order to prevent a spillover of terrorists from across the border. My question is: Do you recall from whom you received this assignment?

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: In the period you mentioned, the company that I commanded at the time was resubordinated to the 125th Motorised Brigade. Sometime on the 26th I was told - I don't remember if it was the commander of the 125th or its Chief of Staff - to report to the forward command post in Djakovica to receive an assignment. After that, I went to Djakovica and I reported to that forward command post. The forward command post -- and I must say, I don't know Djakovica very well although I went there more than once. The forward command post was located somewhere behind the main post office. Those were two buildings, the entrance was between them, and there was something like a cafe or a restaurant in the same building where the forward command post was, but I don't know what it was called. When I arrived, I was of course stopped, in keeping with the procedure, outside the building. I was asked what my business was. I introduced myself. They contacted their superiors and allowed me to proceed into the lobby on the ground floor, where I was again stopped by another guard from the security detail of the forward command post to whom I had to introduce myself again and to state my business. I was told to wait, the time it takes someone to come downstairs from the premises of the forward command post and to escort me upstairs. Somebody from the forward command post came down; I don't recall who it was and I didn't know all of them who worked there, and took me into a room. I said I was there to receive an assignment; however, at that time, if I remember well, the Chief of Staff of the corps was not there, so I had to wait for a while. I can't tell you how long. Anyway, I was waiting in that room, and after a while the Chief of Staff arrived and it was he who gave me that assignment for the dates that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When you say, Mr. Antic, that you received that assignment, was it a written decision or an order in writing for this action?

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: No. The assignment was given me verbally, and I can tell you what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: We have that in your statement. Let's not waste time.

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: Anyway, it was given me verbally.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you receive a map of a decision of some kind?

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: No, no. As I said, it was a verbal assignment. I didn't receive any documents from the Chief of Staff of the forward command post. He just told me what the assignment was, where I was supposed to move and what my destination was, the length of the route, from which point to which point, what had to be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You say the route you were supposed to move on. Of course you were told which route, but how were you able to locate that route?

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: Well, every officer, especially a company commander as well as platoon commanders, have their own topographic maps. It's usually a large-scale map, 1:50.000 or 1:10.000 [as interpreted]. From the beginning of the war from when I began to work at the Pristina Corps from 1993, that is, I had my own map that I was issued with. And on that map I sized up the situation and realized what I was asked to do. Of course, if you'll excuse me, if you are working on a certain segment of the territory, because we were in the zone of responsibility of the 125th Motorised Brigade, sometimes you are given large-scale maps for the specific territory where the unit is located but it's a blank map without any markings, classic, topographic, military map.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Antic. I'll move on now to paragraph 26 where you described in detail the conflict you had, the clash you had, with members of the KLA, and when sunrise came you say on the spot from which the terrorists fired you found a dead terrorist dressed in a camouflage uniform. Did you find anything else on that spot where you found that body and around that place perhaps?

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: In addition to what I stated in my statement and what the terrorist had with him, that is, his personal weapon, an automatic rifle, a hand-held launcher, and a couple of hand-grenades; on the spot from which the terrorists fired at us, at sunrise we found some bloodstains or pools of blood or -- and parts of discarded military equipment, the military vest they used, some ammunition, some parts of military equipment. I can't remember exactly after all this time, but we found bloodstains and military equipment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Two matters just I think at this stage. If you look at line -- or page 6, line 17, you said that you usually had a large-scale map, 1:50.000 or 1 in -- what was the other possible scale?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 25.000. We say a large map in the army, 1:50.000 and 1:25.000 are large maps and they are used for basic units at the level of platoon, company, and such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the other matter is in the paragraph 26 where you refer to arresting three inhabitants of Ramoc, are these the same three people as you had told to stay behind to secure their own houses, or are these different people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are the same three persons from Ramoc. They stayed back, but these are the same persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Antic, in paragraph 27 you state how far your unit got. This is what I want to know: You say your mission was completed about 200 or 300 metres north of Korenica village. Did you get as far as Meja village?

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: No. Meja was not along my axis of operations at all. As far as I remember, in relation to my final destination, Meja was maybe 2 or more kilometres off to the south-east, I mean from the place where I completed my mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Antic, we read your statement and you're telling us today that some components of military police battalion, the component of which you were in command, had been resubordinated at one point to the 125th Motorised Brigade, whereas the remaining components stayed behind to perform security tasks and other tasks that the military police battalion was in charge of. Do you know anything about the fact that at the time you were given this mission and during the actual mission the corps commander, General Lazarevic, was in fact staying in Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: No. I never knew that General Lazarevic, corps commander, ever stayed in that sector or in Djakovica specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I have another question left for you, Mr. Antic. Before you were subordinated to the 125th during the fighting at Kosare, you had been involved in securing the corps command. Can you tell us your impressions of General Lazarevic as a commander. How did he go about issues related to discipline and was he held in high esteem among his soldiers? Tell us if you know, please.

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: The corps commander, General Lazarevic, in my opinion was an exceptional officer, a very fair person and a conscientious professional as well as a model military officer who was always working in keeping with all the military regulations. Since that was the nature of my job, I used to meet quite many generals before the war. I was working in the Pristina Corps territory, and I was performing security tasks there. I know that in terms of cooperation, in terms of how he treated his inferiors, his subordinates, General Lazarevic was the epitome of a professional soldier and he always put service first. I think he even paid more attention than anyone else in his shoes would have to his men, his subordinates and to everything that he was in charge of.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Antic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bakrac. Mr. Ivetic -- sorry, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Antic.

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: My name is John Ackerman. I am one of the lawyers for General Pavkovic in this case. I understand that during your proofing with regard to your testimony that you had an opportunity to observe a video that I think came from the Kosovska Junaci barracks. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes. Over the previous days, I was shown a video clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Just so we have it properly identified in the courtroom and so that you can advise the Chamber that this is the same video that you witnessed, I would like to now play what is 4D18 for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You can continue with playing the video, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think that completes the video, Your Honours. I don't know that there's any need to stay in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We shall return to open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Captain Antic, that video that was just displayed here in court, was that the one that you have previously seen?

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The legend on the video indicates that it was from Kosovska Junaci barracks on the 18th of March, 1999. Were you present at that time?

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And did you hear the remarks that were made by General Pavkovic during his visit to the barracks on that day?

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: said. In the recording, though, I do recognise one of my officers, Lieutenant-Colonel Tegeltija, commander of the 2nd Platoon. He was seated somewhere in that recording.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Do you know if at that time, mid-March of 1999, there was some concern among the ranks of the VJ that there might be a ground attack coming across the border in the near future? Was that something that they were preparing for and concerned about?

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: There was certain indications that there would be an attack coming soon. Any officer, any military man would feel a certain concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would it be an additional concern if you were in a military unit that was facing that border trying to prepare to repel an attack of that nature that there might be KLA units operating behind your units that could attack you from the rear? Would that also be a concern?

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: That would definitely be a concern. Whenever you have the enemy behind your back - I'm referring to what you said about the KLA units - this can always be a problem in terms of you being successful in defending the state border. It can interfere with your tasks, with your defence plans. If indeed it is the case that you have a unit such as a KLA unit behind the back of a unit which happens to be defending the state border.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Antic, sir. My name is Dan Ivetic, and as counsel for Mr. Sreten Lukic I will have just a handful of questions to pose for you today, and they will be dealing with the paragraph 22 of your statement wherein you describe the activities of the 27th and the 28th of April, 1999, in the anti-terrorist action Reka. And I see that the usher has left us. I was going to ask for P615 to be called up, page 21 in e-court, and if possible we could have someone in court assist you to make it more accessible for you to view and perhaps mark on the map that will come up some of the things that I will be asking you so that we can move through this quickly. And for purposes of the map if we could zoom in from the second quadrant on the top on the right side, that is the part that I will be focusing on. Page 21 in e-court. If you can zoom in on the second -- right there, if you could zoom in just a little bit more on that first -- that one square right there all the way to the right. Perfect. Sir, looking at this portion of the map, do you recognise this as being the Reka or Caragoj valley that you mention in paragraph 22 of your statement?

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And I would please beg your indulgence, if you could, to using a red pen which the usher I think will now provide for you, if you could illustrate for us the axis of operations, or [B/C/S spoken], that you describe which you follow-- which was followed by your unit as you say from Dobros to just outside Korenica.

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And could you mark at the beginning of that line the number 52 to denote -- the number of your unit to denote -- because I will be asking for the other participants to be marked according to your knowledge.

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And again, I would beg your indulgence if you could in the same manner depict the direction and the axis of operations of your left neighbouring friendly force, the elements of the 63rd Parachute Brigade. Also marking at that origin point the 63 to denote to differentiate their line from the other lines you will be drawing.

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now with the assistance of the usher I would ask that the colour be changed to blue if it's available so you could depict the same direction and path of -- or axis of operations of your right-hand neighbouring friendly force, the PJP of the Serbian MUP.

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Thank you. Now, we've heard testimony here and from General Zivanovic regarding his 125th Motorised Brigade, and you have also mentioned the 125th. Are you familiar with and are you able to draw in for us the area of blockade that this -- that this unit held during this action I believe from Smonica to Berjan and Nivokaz as General Zivanovic said; are you in a position to be able to mark that on the map in red and with a denotation for 125 to differentiate from the other forces depicted.

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: As for the unit carrying out the blockade, I wasn't given a precise definition of who would be doing what and where. I was only told at the forward command post that some elements from my unit, the 549th and the 125th, those units that were busy securing the state unit would use a minor part of their forces to carry out the blockade west of the Molic-Brovina-Popovac-Sisman road, the road that continues in that general direction. I'm not really able to draw for you with any degree of accuracy what was going on, and I don't know how many men were involved in that particular mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's fine. If we can have -- one moment, please. And I presume just for the sake of clarity what you have just told me would apply also to the units that were located on Cabrat and the elements of the 549th Motorised Brigade as well; is that correct? That you would not be able to accurately depict those on the map and their areas of blockade?

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: Everything that applies to your previous question applies to this one too.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can have this marked as the next available IC number, I can move on with questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be IC172, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Antic, and I thank you for your indulgence in depicting this force. It makes it easier for us to situate ourselves since we were not on the ground there. Now, am I correct, as you have depicted on the map that the forces that were clearing the terrain, your unit, the elements of the 63rd Brigade, as well as the MUP advanced in a line, careful not to intersect their axis of movement during the entire action in the Reka or Caragoj valley?

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: I don't think you're right in at least one way. We weren't clearing the terrain. My mission was to use my forces in order to search the terrain and prevent any spillover of the KLA forces that were operating in the Caragoj or Reka area along my axis of operations only to prevent any spillover by those forces towards the border and any link-up between those forces and those terrorist forces that were operating from Albania into our territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let me try and clarify -- we are at the end -- I apologise, I cannot have the transcript and the map up at the same time due to technical difficulties, that's why I had to pause -- strike back and forth. Would you agree with me that essentially the three elements or forces that are depicted on this map that you've drawn in, these advance of units, if you will, had the same basic assignment just in a particular assigned direction or axis of operation, as I think you called it?

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: I know about my unit and about my mission. I had my own axis of operations which had been assigned to me. This was an axis along which I was to perform my mission. As for what the MUP units involved in this had or my left-hand neighbour, I can only say that I wasn't privy to the detail of their mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Antic, just a couple more questions for you. First of all, with respect to the advancing units that you have drawn in for us on the map, which I again thank you for. During the course of the two days of this action did you have knowledge of any fire being opened up or any combat engagement on the direction of the 63rd Parachute Brigade elements?

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: Do you mean from my left flank or did the KLA take action against the 63rd Parachute Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: I'm not 100 per cent sure, but I think that there were some skirmishes, as mentioned in my case, I think that they had similar cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't understand exactly what that answer amounts to. Are you saying that you could not see Korenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Korenica, as for all of Korenica, from the position where our task ended we could not see Korenica because we were quite literally in the forest, about 300 metres - just a moment, please - about 300 metres to the north-west of Korenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Antic, I would indulge one more question. You mentioned a "vod" or squad in your testimony. Could you tell us the usual numerical strength of a military police "vod," or squad, since I don't think that the denotation has been previously utilised in court?

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: I cannot tell you what is customary, but I can tell you what it is in terms of establishment. In terms of establishment a platoon, "vod," I'm talking about military police units, one platoon has three squads and one squad, "odeljenje," consists of ten men. However, however, if you're asking me specifically about this particular mission, these platoons that I had, or rather, my engaged personnel were incomplete because we had sustained major losses before that in the area of Karaula, Kosare, and Morina, or rather, Rasa and Kosare, so we were insufficiently manned. We did not have enough personnel. We did not have the personnel strength required by establishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your time, and I apologise for any inconvenience it caused you. You I have no further questions for you, Mr. Antic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Antic, you will now be cross-examined by the Prosecutor, Mr. Stamp. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Antic.

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If I could get straight to one of the last things you were saying, and I will try to be very brief with this examination. You were saying that you were about 300 metres from Korenica in a forest. If the village was, in fact, burning, couldn't someone see it from 300 metres? Couldn't someone see the smoke?

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: Maybe someone could see smoke, but there was no smoke. I didn't see any smoke. If there was no smoke, if I did not see any smoke; I don't know if I would have seen it had it been there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You described in your statement the chain of command down to the basic units in your company, and you also said that they were resubordinated to the 125th Brigade in early April. Did you, from time to time, notwithstanding the resubordination, receive commands from Major Kopanja, the battalion commander? Or if I could rephrase that. Did the resubordinated company receive commands from time to time from the battalion commander?

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: While I was there, and I was there two or three times, I cannot say exactly how many days or weeks that was, I did not receive a single order from the --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm afraid I'm not getting translation. Thanks. Yes, could you repeat what you just said. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: While I was there in that area, that is to say with that company that was attached to the 125th, or rather, resubordinated to the 125th Motorised Brigade, I did not receive any orders from the establishment commander of the battalion, that is to say Major Kopanja.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where is the reference to the resubordination, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think it's at paragraph 15 is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And is that the only reference?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: There is an allusion to paragraph 17, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you -- did the resubordinated battalion -- resubordinated company receive any tasks from the head of security, that is, Lieutenant-Colonel, I think it is, Stojanovic, while they were resubordinated to the 125th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: While I was there Colonel Stojanovic, I think he was Colonel Stojanovic, he was a colonel during the war I think, he did not come and see my unit. I did not receive any orders from him. I already told you that we had these shifts in the personnel that was resubordinated to the 125th Brigade. I cannot say whether he came there while somebody else commanded that unit. However, I don't think that Colonel Stojanovic could issue orders. He could only convey an order of the corps commander, convey an order of the corps commander. I really don't ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Wouldn't it be contrary to the procedure in respect of the chain of command for orders to a resubordinated unit, like the company that were resubordinated to the 125th Brigade, to be sent directly to the company from the corps commander?

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: Of course that would not be done directly to the company commander. It would go with the approval of the 125th Motorised Brigade, Colonel Zivanovic; that is to say no one would come directly to the area of deployment of the company that was resubordinated to the 125th and say, Now you're going to do this and that. No, it can't be done that way. One goes to Colonel Zivanovic or to the Chief of Staff, if Colonel Zivanovic is absent, and then together with him -- well, the procedure is that only after that can an order be conveyed with the knowledge and approval of the brigade commander; that is to say the commander of the brigade to which the unit had been attached.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, that is my understanding as well. Could we look at P2297. This is the war diary of the 57th -- of the 52nd Military Police Battalion, and if we quickly take a look at page 6 thereof in English; it is page 9 in B/C/S. On the entry of the 13th of February, 1999, and the reference here is -- that I want to take your attention to is the -- is that it states: "On arrival in the Morina border post sector, we were tasked with the" --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the 13th of February is stated in the translation, question to the witness. In the B/C/S we have the 5th, 6th, and 7th of April, and in English you have the 20th and the 21st of April. Now we have three completely different things and the interpretation of the question said February.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, can you clarify this?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, probably I said February, but when I was reading I think I said the 13th of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let's have the entries for the 13th of April on both sides of the screen, please. MR. STAMP; page 6 in English, page 9 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And it states quite clear there that the unit was tasked by the chief of the security department to capture the border post and that the task was carried out. So you would agree with me, Mr. Antic, that there were occasions when the normal chain of command was bypassed by senior officials or officers in the company -- sorry, in the military police?

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: I could not agree with you because I did not receive such orders. As for this, can I clarify it concerning the 13th?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Go on.

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: This is not the company that I'm talking about. This is a company that had a one-day task, that is to say a task that lasted less than 24 hours, that was sent to the state border at the moment when the terrorists, the terrorist forces, amounting to about 1.000 men, penetrated the first defence line of the state border. So they were urgently sent there as a reinforcement to the units on the first defence line. As for this company, the deputy commander of the battalion, Zeljko Gavrilovic, captain first class, went with this unit, and that's why I leave the possibility -- I allow for the possibility that Colonel Stojanovic conveyed the order to him, that is to say the deputy battalion commander, the deputy of Major Kopanja due to the importance of this mission was sent together with this company to accomplish that task; and that task lasted for less than 24 hours. After that, this unit returned to Pristina and another unit that had already been ready, that had already been ready in the area of disposition of the battalion was sent there and resubordinated to the 125th Motorised Brigade, that is to say at this time and for this unit -- as for the 13th of April, it was not the one that was resubordinated. I allow for the possibility that the order was conveyed to this company because it would be insane to think that even a chief of security would issue an order to a unit without approval and without the knowledge of the corps commander, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So the answer is: This company wasn't resubordinated to the 125th or is there more to the answer than that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This that pertains to the 13th of April that is stated in the diary, that company was not resubordinated to the 125th Motorised Brigade --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Stop there. I can't see why we've heard all this other material unless perhaps someone can clarify it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Not at the moment. Please, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yeah, you have said, however, that Colonel Stojanovic did not have command over the 52nd, he could not task them, but he could only propose the use of the unit, the corps commander, yet we see here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's not my understanding of this, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: At paragraph 7 of his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, I see what you're referring to. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So all I want to know is -- and I think that is your answer. There may be occasions, perhaps emergency situations, when a normal commanding chain may be bypassed, as you described now in emergency situation.

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: If you are trying to tell me that Colonel Stojanovic, or rather, the chief of security sidestepped the corps command or the corps commander and only on his own responsibility engaged these people and issued a task to them, I could not agree with that. He conveyed an order to this unit; that is to say he proposed, that is what is stated in that paragraph of mine. He can make a proposal to the corps commander to the effect that this unit should be used because he is professionally capable of doing that. He makes a proposal, the corps commander approves it, and then Colonel Stojanovic gets that order of the corps commander and he conveys it to Captain Zeljko Gavrilovic, deputy battalion commander, who came with that unit to the actual spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. So it was possible then for senior officers like Colonel Stojanovic and Major Kopanja, the battalion commander, to convey orders from the Pristina Corps command to units that were in the field?

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: In the field, yes, but -- but, please, if they are not resubordinated to another unit -- this unit on the 13th of April was not resubordinated. I told you that during the night another company was sent to be resubordinated to the 125th Motorised Brigade. Yes. That is to say, if a unit goes out on mission independently, then its task is issued to it by the battalion commander or the deputy battalion commander, and this is an order of the corps commander that is conveyed. And if it is resubordinated, then it gets orders from --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we try to keep the answers responsive to the questions that I'm asking and as precise as possible. When the unit was resubordinated to the 125th, was this done in writing? Was there a written order?

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: I'm a company commander. I cannot know that. In most cases I get oral orders, verbal orders, from my commander and certainly there were written orders from the corps command that had arrived to the battalion command, to my commander; however, I as a company commander did not get orders in writing, or rather, before me it was only --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is a very simple question, and I want to keep this short. Was the resubordinate in writing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The answer is I don't know. Please try to confine what you're saying to the particular question that's being asked, and if you don't know the answer to that question there's no point in telling us all sorts of other things. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you see Major Kopanja at any time after you were assigned to the resubordinated company? Do you understand what I'm asking? Perhaps we could -- did you see him after the 21st of April, 1999, at any time?

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: I think I didn't. I think I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So do you know whether or not he visited any of the units that were in the Kosare-Morina area?

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: At the time when I was -- well, as you said, from the 21st Commander Kopanja did not come to the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Before that, before the 21st, while the units were there, do you know if he visited the area?

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: Well, at that time I was in the broader area of Pristina and my task was to secure the corps command, so I don't know whether he went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That was engaged before the 21st in the Morina-Kosare sector; is that so?

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: It was engaged -- well, don't take my word for it, on the 17th, 18th, 19th, those three days. It had intensive combat up there at Kosare.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, that's the significance of the 21st?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The 21st in paragraph 17 of his statement he is saying that is when he, the witness, Mr. Antic, was transferred, as it were, to the area of the Kosare border post.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So this follows but I'll ask you anyway. I take it, therefore,

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: I confirm what I said a few moments ago; namely, I know that from the 21st onwards when I took over the command Kopanja did not come. As for the period before that, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. During the operation or the action in the Caragoj valley, you said that you had in your custody four persons that you handed over to the MUP at some point in time. Were you required at any point in time to make any formal reports to the MUP about the circumstances of their capture or did you merely hand them over and move on?

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: I turned over the four said civilians to the commander of the PJP unit of the MUP, and I told him why I'm turning them over, the reasons why I intercepted them and detained them, and why I'm turning them over for further processing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So you were not required to follow-up on that, to make any formal report, whether within the army or within the -- or to the MUP?

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: Upon completion of the assignment, I informed my superior about the entire assignment, including what I had done with those four.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Orally or in writing?

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: Orally.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Who was that superior?

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: I told you, for that period it was 125th Motorised Brigade; I was resubordinated to them, I informed them, and they passed the report on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was it a person that you informed?

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: I think it was the Chief of Staff of 125th.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The three people that you describe in your statement as the heads of three groups of houses located in the hamlet, were these the patriarchs of three family compounds?

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: They were the elders. You could say patriarchs of the families, although I don't really know; but they were the elders who talked to me and who accepted what I suggested and stayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you suspected that these people were involved in the terrorist action?

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: Since some fire had come from the direction of the houses, that is, from east of the houses, part of the fire directed at us during the night, I suspected that in some way either they fired themselves or they informed KLA members that our positions were there. Anyway, I suspected that somehow they were involved in these events.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, was that -- and this is Ramus?

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: Ramoc, R-a-m-o-c.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thanks. Was that the only village that you went to that you encountered civilians as you came down the mountain?

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: In the course of carrying out this task on the 27th, apart from that one civilian whom we found hiding in the forest, it was my first contact with civilians outside of the village of Ramoc, to the north of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, it was your first contact, but were there -- what I'm asking: Were there any other villages or places that your unit passed through that you had contact with civilians?

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: We had no other contacts with civilians, and my unit moved through an extremely wooded area where there were no houses. It was only outside Ramoc that we came across clusters of houses, two or three in a group, small hamlets you could say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, I think you said in your statement that -- and you also drew it on the map today, that the MUP units were your neighbours to the right and you heard on both days that they were engaged in fighting. Did you see or notice anything to indicate that houses or property was burning in the area to your right?

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: I had not succeeded in establishing either visual or radio contact with the units of the MUP, so I could hear fire from that direction; but I couldn't see what was going on, and I was unable to find out. I did not see smoke coming from the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Apart from -- I'm not sure if I understand what you mean when you say you did not see smoke from the house --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can intervene, as the transcripts going, at lines 14 and 15 I believe the witness said - and you can ask him to verify that - that he did not see smoke or houses ablaze.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see you are nodding. Is that what you're saying, you saw -- the only fire you know of --

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: I said I did not see houses ablaze and I did not see smoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So the only fire you know of during that action was the barn and the haystack outside -- around Ramoc?

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: One haystack caught fire and the fire moved easily to the adjacent part of the structure so that eventually one part of the house also caught fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And that is the only structure you knew of that burnt in the two days that you were involved in this action; is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: That is what I saw and what I know. I did not see or know anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How was this action coordinated? Was there a command post at any place for the VJ units?

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was there a command post at any place for the MUP units?

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you meet with the commanders of the VJ unit to your left and the MUP units to your right before this action started?

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: I had no contact whatsoever with MUP units before the action started all the way until that date, the 28th, and I first met up with the commander of the VJ unit that morning before the action started; and after that, we no longer had any visual contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we look quickly at IC172.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you mean on the 28th or do you mean the 27th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm talking about the 27th, I had no contact with the MUP; and on the 28th, in the morning, just before the assignment started, I met up with the commander of the unit, which was my neighbour on the left. And on the 28th --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters seems to have got this wrong.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 27th in the morning just before the assignment started, I met up with the commander which was my left neighbour and then on the 28th in the morning --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, this is very unclear. Let's start again. You have told us in your statement that the 28th was when you handed over the four persons to the PJP. What you're being asked about just now is when you had discussion to coordinate your work with the PJP. Now, when was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This discussion about coordination of the assignment with PJP did not happen. My first contact with the PJP was around 10.00, 11.00 a.m. On the morning of the 28th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we have a look at IC172.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean this map?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The border to Albania is a broken line to the west of this map, that is, the left, the line that transects on the letter H, is there -- oh, you can't hear?

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, I just wanted to identify the Albanian border.

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: All three units, according to you, were moving down the valley towards Korenica and Meja -- well, your unit was moving towards Korenica. Do I have that correct?

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: My unit went along the route of Dobros-Ramoc towards Korenica but not up to Korenica, towards Korenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. And the -- so I take it, looking at this map, that these three units had a role of pushing terrorists towards Korenica and not blocking the movement to the left or to the west towards Albania; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: Our assignment was to move and search in order to find any terrorists that may be there, and if we find any to arrest them and kill them. So it was not a blockade. It was supposed to be a movement and search of the terrain to find any terrorists in that part of the terrain and to neutralize them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And -- well, what, you searched the forests? Is that all you searched while you came down the valley? Or did you search any village or hamlet or settlement?

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: I told you that on my axis of advance -- look where I am, south of Dobros. On my axis of advance up to Ramoc there were no houses. So I have a certain width, I go along that route, and I try to avoid at all costs -- in this case there weren't any, but if there is no fire from houses you don't perform any detailed search of houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Are you aware that there were convoys or -- let me withdraw the word "convoys" - is that there were groups of civilians moving down the mountain away from your advance towards Korenica?

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: I've already said this. My first contact with civilians was outside Ramoc village. I didn't see any civilians before or after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, but you were in an operation or an action and you were in radio contact. I'm just asking: Did it come to your attention that apart from the civilians who left Ramoc there were convoys of civilians moving away from your advance towards Korenica and Meja? Did you become aware of that?

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: No, nobody informed me about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you become aware or did you know that there were police check-points in the vicinity of Korenica and Meja through which these convoys had to pass?

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: No, no, I had no information about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So as you came down the mountain or came down the valley - and I'm speaking of all three units - were you not told what was the plan in respect to any KLA that would be fleeing in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: The plan was to search the terrain, to find, and to neutralize terrorist forces; that was the plan for my unit, in direct contact, find and neutralize enemy terrorist forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And when you stopped at Korenica, were you not told of any plans for any KLA forces that might have been fleeing in advance of your units and the MUP units?

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: No. I reached my destination, as envisaged in my assignment, I communicated by radio that I had reached my objective and there was nothing further. I was told to return to my prior area of deployment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: About what time on the 28th did you disengage from Korenica or the outskirts of Korenica?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, maybe I jumped before Mr. Stamp corrected himself, disengaged Korenica, meaning the outskirts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was around 3.00, maybe 2.00 p.m. In the afternoon. I can't tell you exactly. At any rate, in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can I move on to just ask you a couple of questions about the video you saw. Do you know what events were occurring at the barracks before that video that you saw -- just saw was created?

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: Before that incident on the video, part of my unit and other parts of the 52nd Battalion of the military police had performed a tactical demonstration exercise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And do you know how long General Pavkovic remained in the barracks that day?

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: I cannot tell you exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So while you were in his presence, did you take notes or take a record of everything that he said?

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: No, I did not. There was no need -- I didn't take any notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. I have nothing further for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp. Mr. Bakrac, you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will have a few questions, but I believe it's time for the break now and the witness does need a rest because of his leg. I'll be very brief after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before we have our break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Antic, have you ever heard of a unit called the 14th Counter-Intelligence Group?

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, we need to have a break at this stage and that break will last for about half an hour. Just you remain where you are at the moment until we've left the bench, and the usher will show you where you can wait and make yourself comfortable while we have this break. We will resume at 11.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Antic, I only have three more questions for you, so I shan't be too long, additional ones. Can we please have Exhibit IC172 brought up on our screens. Mr. Antic, you drew the route along which you were moving and part of the 63rd as well. First of all, let me ask you this: How strong was this component of the 63rd Parachute Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: There was a component of the 63rd Parachute Brigade that was about as strong as my own forces. I can't say precisely, but I don't think it was more than 30 or 40 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you. Where were they to complete their mission? How far were they supposed to get on the 28th, if you could please point that out to us, that's why I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, their mission was to be completed approximately where I drew this line near Ripaj-Madanaj, give or take a hundred metres, but it was in that belt.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Antic, I have another question. Mr. Stamp asked you about when these persons surrendered or were surrendered, and he asked you about some documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we didn't know that this issue would be raised on the cross, and I found during the break the methods on the combat use of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with that textbook?

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is a book that is used for training ordinary soldiers and officers of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Is there anything there that envisages the manner in which non-military persons are surrendered when the situation is of military interest?

utterances.speaker: SASA ANTIC
utterances.text: This is something that is envisaged under the heading: Bringing persons in, so these civilian persons, non-military persons, are to be handed over to bodies of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I will read out a sentence very briefly, and you tell me whether this is one of the methods described in the book. "Non-military persons or foreigners" --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Is this an exhibit and this is quite leading as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, is it an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours, I just found this. I was prompted to do this by Mr. Stamp's question on cross-examination, but I will be tendering this as a bar table exhibit at a later stage, these methods. We didn't realize that this would be raised or challenged. Just a single sentence for the witness to confirm whether this is, indeed, a sentence from that book, not -- or perhaps I should let the witness read this for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it's a pointless exercise, Mr. Bakrac. It would be a leading question at this stage. The witness has told us what he did, and what you want to do is demonstrate that this is consistent with the practice set down in this book, well you can do that by tendering it at the bar table. There's no need to ask any questions. Move to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will be tendering this as a bar table exhibit. I agree with you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Antic. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this completes my re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Antic, that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming here to the Tribunal to give evidence. You may now leave the courtroom. The usher will show you where you can now go.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And to ensure that that is effective, the statement itself should be admitted under seal for the moment. So you would have to consider not only the transcript but the statement, and you should make your position clear on that by the end of this week.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour, that will be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bakrac, who is the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the next witness is Pavle Gavrilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do similar issues arise in relation to his evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So how do you suggest we deal with Gavrilovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: The safest measure is to take it completely in private; however, I know that the Court is loathed to do that so we just have to monitor. We can talk about general operations, but to the extent that we are going to talk about any comparison of testimony, that has to be going into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If and when the statement is admitted, then you suggest it should be on the basis that paragraphs 15, 18, and 20 are redacted?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And we should start on the basis that we are hearing the evidence in public and counsel should draw our attention to the situation, should it be likely that references would lead to the identity of any of the protected witnesses who have given evidence on these subjects. Is that the position?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, that sounds sensible. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You will be cautious and alert us should there be any need to go into private session. We shall now return to open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you have just confirmed to us, Mr. Bakrac, that the next witness will be Pavle Gavrilovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the next witness for the Lazarevic Defence is Pavle Gavrilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Gavrilovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You will now be examined by Mr. Bakrac on behalf of Mr. Lazarevic. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Gavrilovic, good morning. Please state your full name for the record, tell us your date and year of birth and your place of birth.

utterances.speaker: PAVLE GAVRILOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Pavle Gavrilovic. I was born on the 31st of January, 1965, in Pirot.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Gavrilovic, you will have to make a pause for me to ask you a question, that gets interpreted, and then you start answering; and please slow down so the interpreters can interpret accurately what you are saying. Mr. Gavrilovic, did you not make a statement to the Lazarevic Defence team on the 9th of January, 2008?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE GAVRILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to read that statement and sign it?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE GAVRILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Is the statement an accurate reflection of what you told the Lazarevic Defence team?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE GAVRILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Were I to ask you the same questions today about all the topics that you covered in your statement, would you still provide the same answers, sir?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE GAVRILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Or rather, Mr. Gavrilovic, we all have your statement in front of us. We have the opportunity to familiarise ourselves with its substance and there is no need to repeat any of this. I will be asking you one thing, though. We shall try to furnish some additional clarifications for the benefit of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have a couple of questions and these are questions about the evidence given by these witnesses, or rather, I apologise, just before I go there. I didn't give you the exhibit number for the statement and I did not move that it be admitted. This is 5D1397.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can it please be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: The Prosecution requests that this be under seal until a redacted version is provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're not content that we simply have the three paragraphs under seal that you identified?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: That is fine --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I see what you're suggesting, that that's the practical way of doing it. Yes, you're quite right. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, let me just check if we're in private session now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, we are in open session. Do you want to go into private session? Yes. Very well. 10 [Private session] [Confidentiality partially lifted by later order of the Chamber]

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: (redacted) Were any of the combat groups stationed in a village and were any of the combat groups stationed in the village of Damjane?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE GAVRILOVIC
utterances.text: There was a combat group that was stationed in Damjane, not in the village itself but rather near the village. I was the commander of the logistics battalion and there was a component of my unit that was in that combat group, that was part of that combat group. I visited them several times then and other combat groups that were deployed across these sectors. But none of the components were in the actual village, they were in the village, around the village, if you like. My own component was in the tents and food was prepared in the open air. I'm not sure if that's what your question was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I'll interrupt you now because we're using up too much time for explanations that are not strictly necessary.

utterances.speaker: PAVLE GAVRILOVIC
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Were there any civilians in that village? Did they remain or did the soldiers drive them out and didn't they tell them to go to their homes?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE GAVRILOVIC
utterances.text: The civilians stayed there and nobody ever told them to go or drag them out.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Since you were the commander of that battalion, say you appointed someone to be the driver of a particular combat group, would this person not be in charge of distributing food and other necessities to other combat groups as well?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE GAVRILOVIC
utterances.text: No. If I may just explain briefly. This person would have been in charge of that specific combat group and his only responsibility would be to furnish supplies for that unit, food and water specifically. He would not have been able to bring supplies to any other combat group but his own.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: This witness also said that in 1998 he was ordered to take the lorries that were still road-worthy and to seize them for military purposes.

utterances.speaker: PAVLE GAVRILOVIC
utterances.text: No, that never occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you seize any lorries back in 1998 when the war broke out?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE GAVRILOVIC
utterances.text: No, none.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you have any civilian lorries?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE GAVRILOVIC
utterances.text: There were some vehicles that had been left behind, abandoned, but this wasn't the case in my unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you have any vehicles that had been mobilised for your purposes?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE GAVRILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we had a number of vehicles that had been mobilised, but those came together with drivers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Gavrilovic, this same witness also gives evidence about an action early in March 1999 in Jeskovo village. You were the commander of the logistics battalion, were you not? In your capacity as commander of that battalion, did you know that any component from your unit took part, took an active part, in the action in the village of Jeskovo in March 1999?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE GAVRILOVIC
utterances.text: No, definitely not. Perhaps in the sense of providing the logistic, but certainly not in any active role.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When you say in terms of providing logistics, what exactly do you mean?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE GAVRILOVIC
utterances.text: I mean supplying food and drinking-water.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Assume there is an action that is supposed to last maybe one or two days, what is the procedure regarding food and water?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE GAVRILOVIC
utterances.text: If it takes no more than one or two days, then there is no need for these supplies to be provided. Each soldier would have been expected to carry their rations on them and whatever the amount of water was that they were likely to be using up as well as their ammunition. There is no need to provide any additional supplies and my unit was not called upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And when supplies were necessary, how many soldiers would normally be required and how would they get there?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE GAVRILOVIC
utterances.text: When supplies were required, no matter if food or water, normally there would be a vehicle with a driver and an officer in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Were they authorised to leave the vehicle, to leave the vehicle behind, and enter an area of combat operations?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE GAVRILOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You're providing very brief answers now. This is going well somehow, but I asked you to make a pause for my question to be interpreted first. Now we're getting along just fine because the answers are brief, but if they get any longer we might be facing some interpretation trouble. Mr. Gavrilovic, you were the commander of the logistics battalion. Was it ever the case that a water tanker was found at the head of a combat column just behind a tank?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE GAVRILOVIC
utterances.text: No, that would have been impossible.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this point I'm not clear where in the 65 ter summary or in the statement that these subjects are being discussed. I think we've gone outside of the summaries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't think this exceeds the context of the summary. This witness is telling us about the evidence given by two other witnesses in relation to a particular incident. We're in closed session, in Trnje village, and he's supposed to say something about the evidence of these two witnesses,(redacted); and they talk about this detail, I mean Jeskovo, in their respective statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where is the reference to Jeskovo in his statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is none in his statement, but I think there is mention of the fact that he would be commenting on the evidence of (redacted). That's in the 65 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I'm looking at your 65 ter statement and I don't think I see that, but it's in the statement -- it's in his statement that he will be commenting on the evidence of (redacted), but also the 65 ter statement doesn't appear to refer to Jeskovo either.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And respectfully, Your Honour, when he is supposed to be commenting on the other two witnesses' materials, that he's very specific in regards to it's the March incidents and just generally rebutting specific statements made by the witnesses, as opposed to some general overview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In any event, you've -- the question that you did ask has been answered, Mr. Bakrac. Now, please continue but confine yourself to what you've given notice of raising.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Gavrilovic, this same witness, (redacted), speaking of the blockade above Jeskovo village, says that among others the soldiers who entered Trnje village in order to conduct a search of that village, there was also Private Dejan Milosevic. Do you know Private Dejan Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE GAVRILOVIC
utterances.text: Private Dejan Milosevic is familiar to me. I know him because he wasn't entirely fit for military service, but he still joined the ranks. He was with the technicians, he worked there as a mechanic. He had some trouble walking, he wasn't properly able to walk, and I am entirely certain that he was certainly not away from this unit. This is entirely impossible that he would have gone anywhere like that because he wasn't entirely able --

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- to walk. I know him, I know his name, this is a soldier from Pristina who --

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Respectfully, Your Honour, again we are falling in the same trap, that is that I don't see anywhere in the 65 ter summary or within the statement itself with regards to (redacted) that begins at paragraph 20, and there's no mention whatsoever of this incident, this person, or this topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it certainly was mentioned, and in chief the witness testifies about that. According to (redacted), Dejan Milosevic did take part in the action in the village of Trnje. You have that on page 3 of his statement in B/C/S --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that, Mr. Bakrac. The objection is that you haven't given notice that this witness would be specifically dealing with these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, in 65 ter we did give a more general picture -- rather, a warning, an indication that we would be dealing with the testimonies of these witnesses regarding the village of Trnje. That is precisely what I am talking about now. Clearly in relation to all the things that these witnesses said about the incident in Trnje --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, please show me in the 65 ter summary where you refer to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is paragraph 5, paragraph 5, that's the action of deblocking the road between Suva Reka and Prizren. We did announce that, the activities of the 549th Motorised Brigade in destroying Siptar terrorist forces in the deblockade of Retimlje and the Suva Reka-Orahovac road. This is an action that went on for four days, and that is what these two witnesses testified about. As a matter of fact, what was shown to them were these analyses, they were shown to them by the OTP regarding the command of the Pristina Corps. It is a Prosecution exhibit, and it specifically has to do with this particular blockade or rather the participation of this witness in that, in that action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Carter, both these witnesses identified or made reference to this witness in the course of their evidence. Although the 65 ter lacks specification, it's not necessary that it should be specific to the points that you raise unless they were discreet points, and here there is notice that he will be dealing with that particular action. So we shall allow this questioning to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Gavrilovic, I think that you have answered my previous question. At any rate, tell me, you described in detail in your statement your participation in blocking the terrain in the action on deblocking this road.
