utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. That's fine. I just need the last page of this document, the last page to see who it was delivered to.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So my learned friend Ms. Carter showed you paragraph G about the clean up of the battle-field. Please look at the very bottom of the document, the left-hand corner, you don't have to read this back to us, we can see who it was delivered to. But my question is: Was this order at all delivered to your logistics battalion?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE GAVRILOVIC
utterances.text: No, I said so, didn't I, a while ago, I mean ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Gavrilovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions for this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Respectfully, Your Honour, with regards to P1981 the reason it was under seal is because it came in with one of the protected witnesses. We saw no reason for the document to remain under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. We shall lift the seal on that document. Just before we finish, could you look at paragraph 5.6 of that document, please. Can you magnify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you read aloud, please, paragraph -- well, the first two lines of paragraph 5.6.

utterances.speaker: PAVLE GAVRILOVIC
utterances.text: "Blockade at the line. TT 357 Trnje village," probably "Jezero facility, Mistra facility TT 330, Smac village TT 316, Donja Srbica village. Ceramija [phoen] carried out by parts of the logistics battalion, signals company HAD and parts of SART PVO."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What does HAD mean?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE GAVRILOVIC
utterances.text: SART PVO self-propelled rocket artillery battalion of the anti-aircraft defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what does SART PVO stand for?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE GAVRILOVIC
utterances.text: That's it, SART PVO. That's what I said. I don't know what the interpretation was, but I'm looking at the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, the interpretation was something rather different, but it all relates to the one unit. Thank you very much. Mr. Gavrilovic, that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming to give evidence. You may now leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Our next witness is Mr. Radomir Mladenovic. In the meanwhile we informed OTP and other lawyer and subject of colleagues that Mr. Mladenovic will testify live one hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I need to be excused for about three minutes and there's no reason you can't go forward without me, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you very much. Good afternoon, Mr. Mladenovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please take a seat. You will now be examined by Mr. Cepic on behalf of Mr. Lazarevic. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Esteemed colleague, for the benefit of the transcript, please state your full name.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Radomir Mladenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When and where were you born?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: I was born on 10th of July, 1960, in the village of Srezovce, which is in Kosovo and Metohija, Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: I am a national of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mladenovic, tell us about your educational background.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: I graduated from the law faculty in Sarajevo, and then I took the bar exam in Belgrade after that, the top schools.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mladenovic, what do you do today?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Since May 2005 I have been working as a district judge in Nis. I still hold the same post.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: That judicial system works in a different way and there are several different kinds of judges. What exactly do you do in your capacity as district judge?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: I am the president of the so-called trial chamber, I preside over a trial chamber that rules on any charges submitted by the district prosecutor in Nis.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What kind of law are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Criminal law.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I will ask you one thing, sir. When I ask a question and you start your answer, please make a short pause before your answer so that everything may be entered into the transcript accurately. Mr. Mladenovic, which post were you holding back in 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: In 1998 and all the way up to the beginning of the war, I was a judge with the military court in Nis.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: When the war broke out and during the war, what was your responsibility?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: When a state of war was declared, I was assigned to Pristina. During the war I worked as president of the military court that was attached to the Pristina Corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps remember on which date you took up your duty there?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: On the 25th of March when a state of emergency was declared I reported to Pristina. At first there had been a decree to appoint me the president of the military court of the commands of the Pristina Military District. On the 25th I reported and we set up this court, I mean the military district court. And then on the 27th of March, three days later, I was informed that by presidential decree, federal presidential decree, I had been appointed president of the military court of the Pristina Corps command. I took up my post on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During the war, how many military courts were there in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: There were two that were operating, the one where I served as president, the one that was attached to the Pristina Corps command; and there was another one attached to the Pristina Military District command, so those were the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: In terms of jurisdiction, over what persons did you have jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: I can tell you about the military court that was attached to the Pristina Corps command, although I do know what the other one had jurisdiction over as well. According to the rules governing the work of military courts in a state of war, the courts that were set up and were attached to certain commands - in this specific case the Pristina Corps command had jurisdiction over criminal matters when crimes were committed by military persons who were members of the corps, and also in relation to some crimes committed by civilians against the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: The court attached to the command of the military district has what jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: That court also had jurisdiction over all members of the district, military personnel, that is, and civilians who committed crimes against the Army of Yugoslavia or its members.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: In the territory of Kosovo and Metohija during the war there were other units as well, including units of air force and anti-aircraft defence. These two courts that you mentioned, did they have jurisdiction over the members of air force and anti-aircraft defence?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: No. Those were under the jurisdiction over a court attached to the command of air force and anti-aircraft defence. However, for purposes of expediency and efficiency, it was possible for a higher court, the supreme military court, to send a delegation of our corps court to adjudicate such matters, but only along the principles of delegation at the proposal of the prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I will dwell a bit longer on jurisdiction. You said that the military court had jurisdiction over any crime against the Army of Yugoslavia. If, for example, a civilian had admitted a criminal act against a member of the Army of Yugoslavia who was not on duty at the moment, which court had the jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: In that case, a regular civilian court would have jurisdiction. The military court would have jurisdiction only if the crime was committed against the member of the Army of Yugoslavia on duty. In every other case, the civilian court would be in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What about members of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Well, members of the Ministry of the Interior, the police, are not military personnel, and the law governing the military courts stipulates that military courts have jurisdiction over military personnel, enumerating them by category. Policemen are not listed there. Therefore, the court that I presided over did not try members of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Who was in charge of them?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Regular courts in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I just wanted to learn something. Kindly tell me if a case like a sabotage had taken place or something against the state which attracts military law and there's a civilian with a military person, will such a case also go to a civilian court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the criminal act of sabotage is involved targeting military installations or military personnel, then the military court would have jurisdiction. If other facilities are involved, then the military court is not in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: There's a question that I wish to ask just to follow-up on that one. What if in the event a member of the police had committed an offence against a member of the military, would the military court have jurisdiction in that case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that kind of case, military court has exclusive jurisdiction because the military court has jurisdiction in all cases where the injured party is a military person; however, only if that person was on duty. If he got into a brawl with a soldier somewhere in a bar, then the military court would have nothing to do with it because the soldier was not on duty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: So just when he's acting in the course of his duties but not in a personal capacity, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry to keep you back, Mr. Cepic. I don't think you answered one aspect of Judge Chowhan's question, which was: If you have a military person who is serving at the time, on duty, commits -- committing a crime along with a civilian against a civilian, is it the military court or the civilian court which has jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That depends on the mode of complicity. If they are accomplices, then the military court has some jurisdiction considering that one of the perpetrators is a military person, if they are co-perpetrators; and the military court remains in charge always in such cases. If they committed a crime against civilians as co-perpetrators, then the military court also tries the civilian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, again about jurisdiction, did civilian courts operate during the war?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I know that in Kosovo and Metohija during the state of war there were five district courts and 19 municipal courts, and they all operated.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I know it is very difficult to express this in figures or in a ratio, the relationship between military and civilian courts in terms of actual or personal jurisdiction, but can you try?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: If we bear in mind that these two courts in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, figuratively speaking, were supposed to try members of the Pristina Corps, I don't know what the strength of the Pristina Corps was at the time, let's say 50 to 60.000, and if we take it that there were certainly over a million citizens of age in Kosovo and Metohija in total, then you can use it for purposes of comparison.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mladenovic, during this trial it was emphasised that there was a request to resubordinate MUP forces to the army, and it was not implemented. Several witnesses stressed that. Legally speaking, if resubordination had happened, would officers of the army have been able to discipline members of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think so because disciplinary liability in the army is governed by the Rules of Service and the Rule of Military discipline. Members of the MUP and their disciplinary liability is regulated by the Law on Internal Affairs. And during the war there was a decree governing disciplinary liability. Second, as far as military personnel is concerned, a soldier can be punished by detention; an officer can be convicted to two months in military prison by a military disciplinary court, whereas these sanctions were not applicable to members of the MUP. That's why I believe it would be incompatible.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mladenovic. Very briefly, let's try to clarify one point that perhaps remained unclear in prior testimony. Which laws governed substantial criminal law?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: At the level of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, there was the criminal law, the penal code of the FRY, and each republic, Serbia and Montenegro, had their own penal codes. The federal penal code stipulated such things as basic criminal acts, criminal liability, and sanctions, but republics also -- for instance, the federal law dealt with crimes against military personnel, and the federal law also dealt with crimes in federal authorities, whereas republican laws dealt with criminal acts against persons acting in an official capacity.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: In federal and in republican laws, both, we find the same criminal acts. If a military person commits a crime prescribed by these two laws, which law applies, the federal or the republic law?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: In the federal law we don't have classic crimes against property. We have laws that deal with property offences that are very grave and concern official property. Republic laws regulate theft, property, et cetera. For instance, if you have the crime of abuse of official authority that results in embezzlement and things like that, then that is regulated by the federal law; but that is a criminal act which has property feature.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Abuse of official authority is also governed by a republic law, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: But if a military person commits such a crime, which law applies?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: The federal law should apply because that military person is at the same time an authorised officer in a federal agency because the Army of Yugoslavia is a federal agency, a federal institution, and that's why the federal law would apply.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mladenovic, who had the authority to file criminal reports?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: In principle, anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If an officer of the army reports a crime, where does his obligation stop in relation to further processing of that crime?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: It ends with the act of reporting it. It would even be inappropriate for him to try to inquire any further or to try to influence the process any further because the matter is from that point on in the hands of the competent authorities such as the military courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: To make this absolutely clear because we are coming from a different judicial system, could you explain various phases of proceedings that precede the indictment?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: According to our Law on Criminal Procedure, we are talking now about the relevant period of the indictment, year 1999, it is the prosecutor that receives criminal reports. When he receives a criminal report with various appendices, the prosecutor has to evaluate whether there is a well-grounded suspicion that the allegations are true. And if the prosecutor decides that there is a prima facie case then he will ask the competent investigative judge to conduct an investigation; and the investigation already falls into the category of pre-criminal proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: So how many stages are there?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Before the indictment, there is the so-called pre-criminal phase that the investigative judge conducts with the police and other authorities. Then there is the preliminary proceedings, which is already in the category of court proceedings. After that, if the evidence is sufficient, the prosecutor issues an indictment which is subject to verification by three judges, in case there are any objections. When the indictment enters into force, the trial can proceed and those were the stages at the time we are discussing.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: In response to my previous question you said that the judicial authorities were independent in their work and free of any influence from outside. I would like to know whether there were any attempts to influence your work and the work of the judges of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: I was a judge of the military court in Nis for 11 years. It never ever happened that anyone influenced me or attempted to do that. It was more of a 11 case where someone, if I may say so before Your Honours, a friend of mine, on 12 what they call a friendly basis asked for help for one accused or someone 13 else. But as for officers from various commands, that certainly never 14 happened. [Defence counsel confer]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I don't think we have proper interpretation of your previous answer. I'll ask you a brief question and you give me a brief answer, please. Did anyone during the war try to influence you or other judges of the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think we'll have a formal translation by CLSS --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- of page 109, lines 8 -- sorry -- yes, line 22 to 25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, there's a little more I just want to learn about your system. How were the cases assigned if there were more than one court, who did it and what was the criteria? And secondly, did anybody ask you for a progress report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Cases were assigned depending on when the criminal reports reached the appropriate office. I'm not sure if you can hear me. I'm not sure what reports you have in mind. Our duty was to inform the superior court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: The entrustment of cases if there are more judges, who would entrust case to which one I mean, who was in charge of entrustment or marking of cases to a court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During the state of war, the Pristina Corps court had three investigating judges and four of those who tried the actual cases. I was one of those four because I was the president of that court. Cases were assigned on the following basis: A sequence would be established in terms of when they got there, when they reached the registry of the court. I was given one case as the president and then the next judge and then the next judge, one by one; so that was the system that we used. What I'm trying to say is this, there was no particular sequence. It's not that cases were selected specially in order to be assigned to someone. This is exactly what the rules say, too, that cases should be assigned and tried in the order in which they are received. My apologies. Just another additional explanation. As for investigations, it really depended on who the investigative judge happened to be who was on a certain case [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. May I continue? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mladenovic, how many cases did you handle personally during the war?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: I do remember because I continued to work for the military court in Nis after the war, immediately after the state of war was declared over. I drafted reports for myself and for the supreme military court, and I know that during the war we conducted investigations of about 8.000 [as interpreted] persons, over 900 of those being indicted eventually.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, page 111, 12; I believe the witness says: It depended on who of the investigative judges happened to be on duty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And one more error in transcript, page 111, line 20, investigation about 8.000, it is not 8.000, witness said 1.000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mladenovic, if you were dealing with crimes that potentially constituted violations of the international laws of war, how many indictments like that did you have? I know that you can't be all that specific.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: About 230 over a total of these 900 that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What kind of crimes predominantly?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Various forms of murder, robbery, theft, aggravated theft, vehicles being seized, crimes against personal dignity and morale, sex-related offences.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps remember how many officers were prosecuted for such crimes, not ordinary soldiers, officers?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: If you look at both these military courts a total of about 40 military officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Mladenovic, we heard evidence several days ago in this courtroom about a major of the VJ Dragisa Petrovic, more specifically it was said that along with another two soldiers, he committed murder. Are you perhaps familiar with this case?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps know what the conviction was by the Supreme Court?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Major Dragisa Petrovic got nine years and the two soldiers got seven each. They are all now serving their sentence at the correctional penal institute in Nis.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Mladenovic, were there any crimes that were discovered after the war?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Indeed. After the war when the peacetime military court in Nis had already started operating, to call it that, requests for investigations started arriving about crimes such as the ones that we have been discussing.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the Mancic case?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Were any rape cases tried later on?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: No, not later on. There was a rape case involving three soldiers who were indicted during the war, sometime in May 1999, I believe. They were accused of having raped three young ladies. They were on remand at the time. I was the one who went forward with this indictment, and I am privy to its detail. If you want to know more, just say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Mladenovic, what about after the war, were there any problems in terms of gathering evidence for trials?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. If I may, I would like to refer once more to the case that we discussed a minute ago, the rape case. Those young ladies who were victims could not be interviewed while we were still in Kosovo and Metohija. As president of that chamber, I appealed to the international authorities and the local authorities in Kosovo and Metohija, as well as the civilian courts, to try to interview those young ladies or maybe to have them escorted to the military court in Nis so that I might be given a chance to interview them. Unfortunately, all of our appeals were turned down. And after the military court in Nis was abolished, the case was forwarded to another civilian court.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What about other investigations, did the same problems occur in relation to the gathering of evidence in any other investigations?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, especially during the first two or three years after the war. It was always risky to try to get anything at all from Kosovo and Metohija. Secondly, the postal system was not operating properly and the communications system; therefore, it was very difficult to handle these cases before the military court in Nis.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Did you submit any requests within your own administration system, requests for assistance?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, both in the case that we mentioned a while ago and in the Mancic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have Exhibit 3D1061. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may, there's a part of my question that wasn't recorded. May I please repeat the question just in order to clarify?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mladenovic, did you submit requests to the UNMIK administration and the legal authorities in Kosovo and Metohija for assistance in these cases?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: In the rape case the answer is yes; as for the more recent one, I appealed to the district court in Prizren for assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What sort of cooperation did you have?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Sometime in July last year I sent them a letter in order to continue to go on with the trial all the way up until December last year. I never received anything in return, so the trial was deferred until March because I believe that they might, given more time, forward the documents that we had requested.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please look at the document that is on our screens.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have looked at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: During your -- before I proofed you, had you ever seen this document?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Is this the sort of information that affected any proceedings or is this the kind of information that you ever received that was delivered to you?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: No, this sort of information was never delivered to us, and I don't think they could have affected proceedings in any way, especially as far as this was concerned, the proceedings that were underway before the military court in Nis.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: The English translation is not really crystal clear, but there's a reference here to the fact that there were suspicions that members of the TG 2 or members of the Lipljan MUP had committed this crime, and the village mentioned there is Mali Alas. Are you familiar with that village, sir?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What can you tell me about this village?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: I learned everything that I learned in my official capacity as the president of the court that was attached to the corps. I learned that the military prosecutor, who was also attached to the corps command, having learned of this incident went to the area to carry out an on-site investigation. And he requested the court to launch an investigation in order to shed light on the circumstances under which these civilians had come to grief. They thought that maybe during the investigation they might track down the perpetrators, or rather, that was the purpose of the steps that were taken. And then we pressed on. Our forensic team, a team of experts from the military medical academy, was sent to the site. There was an investigating judge who was in charge of the team that carried out the exhumation work, and this was something that was handled during the war and later by the military court in Nis.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have Defence Exhibit 5D1313.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you move on, Mr. Cepic, is that translation accurate at line 18 of page 115, "this sort of information was never delivered to us and I don't think they could have affected proceedings ..." What's being said here, is it inappropriate for the military prosecutor to forward this material? If the interpretation's accurate, then I will ask some questions myself, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness is a judge and not a prosecutor, and the interpretation is correct because a judge is not the same thing as a prosecutor and they are independent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Mladenovic, looking again at the document again on the screen, why would you never receive this sort of information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I said was that I did not receive this information specifically --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that, but the translation says: "This sort of information was never delivered to us ..." So you're confining that answer to this information in this particular case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'm talking about this specific case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That clarifies it. Thank you very much. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I apologise for a little bit wrong explanation and clarification of this material. Could we have 5D1313, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mladenovic, what is this document, the one that we're looking at?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: It is precisely what I was talking about. A forensic examination was carried out on the bodies of those people who had been killed, and minutes were drawn up or a report was drawn up.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mladenovic, this is page 2, we see the date, we see the time, we see the name of Major Ivica Milosavljevic, Milos Kostov, and all the other ones. Okay now, if you can please explain about this person Zoran Saveljic. Who was he?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: This was a judge of the military court attached to the Pristina Corps command, and he ordered for this explanation to go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In addition to this location, was there another location that was found nearby?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember a place that I think was called Slovinje.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have 5D1315. Could we have the second page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you ever receive this letter, Mr. Mladenovic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I received it in my Pristina office, and there were photographs attached to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, for the sake of expedience, there is an attachment to this document containing the photographs and the technical details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mladenovic, the final question: Are you aware whether any of the perpetrators of this crime were eventually found?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: It wasn't until later when I worked with -- at the Nis military court that I found out through the media that a prosecutor was pressing charges against some local Serbs from that village.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... 5D1366, please. We miss one word on page 118, line 25 -- actually, the next line, 119, line 1, UN mission, UNMIK prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Instead of media -- sorry, from the media that an UNMIK prosecutor was pressing charges. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: As far as charges being pressed against, what did you hear at the time?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Some local Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mladenovic, what about this document that's in front of you, does it not appear to confirm what you heard? I showed it to you during proofing.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether you were involved in their work, but during the proofing?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's the exhibit number for that document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this might be a good time. I see that my learned friends are getting a little restless.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Mladenovic, we have to terminate our proceedings for today at this stage, which means that you will have to come back tomorrow to complete your evidence. That will be at 2.15 tomorrow in courtroom number 3. So please be back in time ready to resume your evidence at that stage. You can now leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Until tomorrow at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 29th day of January, 2008, at 2.15 p.m. 21 22 23 24
